source.title: Projecting Assumptions: The Duality Between Sparse Autoencoders and Concept Geometry
source.citation: Sai Sumedh R. Hindupur et al., 2025
source.authors: Sai Sumedh R. Hindupur; E. Lubana; Thomas Fel; Demba E. Ba

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling, cutoff, or wrong-document issue.
record.tranche_reason: The study’s theory and experiments refine claims about SAE feature recovery: they show architecture-specific assumptions can cause concepts to be missed, and that concepts can have heterogeneous intrinsic dimensions. It does not test superposition itself.
record.gate_note: The study compares SAE architectures and measures their concept recovery and representation geometry. It does not test whether sparse features are stored as overlapping directions under capacity pressure, or whether model neurons become polysemantic because of that pressure. Statements about prior work are not recorded as results. The formal-language experiment is described as semi-synthetic and uses a 2-layer Transformer trained from scratch, not a naturalistic large language model.
record.test_reason: The study trains ReLU, JumpReLU, TopK and SpaDE SAEs on synthetic clusters, a 2-layer PCFG Transformer and DINOv2 activations. It shows that which concepts an SAE recovers depends on its architecture. This is a results-based argument against SAE features being complete or canonical units (V5). The formal-language experiment also measures that parts of speech occupy subspaces of differing dimension, which bears weakly on V6. It does not test superposition itself (V1–V4).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that each SAE architecture imposes implicit assumptions about concept geometry, so it can miss or mix concepts that violate them. Different SAEs are not interchangeable, no single SAE is universally optimal, and geometry-aware design (SpaDE) improves concept specialization.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce or apply the Toy Models of Superposition method; it develops and evaluates a framework for SAE architectures and concept geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Concept recovery varies with SAE architecture and sparsity level. In the formal-language experiment, F1 peaks at different sparsity levels by concept for ReLU and JumpReLU; the number of dimensions represented by TopK must be chosen relative to concept dimension.
record.problems: The paper tests two synthetic setups, a semi-synthetic formal-language model, and a 10-class vision subset; it does not test naturalistic LLMs for the LLM-specific claim version. Several comparisons are described qualitatively in the text without exact values. The text does not report seed-to-seed stability tests for canonicality.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows omitted. Figure-only values without a textual description were not transcribed as numbers.

untested.parts: No toy superposition model, sparsity-dependent phase transition or geometry of superposed directions.
No test of neuron polysemanticity arising from capacity competition.
No test of the causes of neuron polysemanticity in the underlying model.
No LLM. Only a small PCFG Transformer and DINOv2, and no measurement of how features spread across neurons.
No seed-to-seed stability or SAE-width/scale tests, and no LLM setting.
Only cumulative-variance dimension of PoS clusters. No test of whether multi-dimensional concepts are irreducible, and no superposition setting.

missing.what: TopK in the formal-language setup crosses 5% normalized MSE at different k for each PoS. No row records this.
Per-class F1 values for each SAE on DINOv2, and ReLU/JumpReLU F1 varying across classes (no row for the non-SpaDE SAEs' F1).
Dead-latent fractions and stable ranks: the other SAEs fall well below the target stable rank of 6, while SpaDE is high.

record.verdict_notes: The study does not reproduce the original Toy Models of Superposition source. The synthetic experiments use no model, only designed Gaussian data, so they speak to SAE recovery of ground-truth concepts rather than to model features. Comparisons are partly unequal: SpaDE's hyperparameters are fixed, while the other SAEs in the formal-language setup report best-of-sweep results, which favours the baselines.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment tests superposition, feature sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometric arrangements of overlapping directions.
No experiment tests neuron polysemanticity as competition for limited representational capacity or compares dedicated dimensions with shared ones.
The study reports SAE-latent co-occurrence, not polysemanticity of the underlying model’s neurons, and does not test whether that phenomenon is evidence for superposition.
The formal-language model is a small Transformer trained from scratch in a semi-synthetic setup; the study does not test feature distribution across neurons or SAE recovery in naturalistic LLMs.

The study tests architecture-dependent concept recovery and argues against universal or interchangeable SAE features. It does not test seed-to-seed stability or establish whether any particular SAE gives a complete, canonical account of a model’s representation.
The study tests whether concepts can have heterogeneous, multidimensional structure, but does not study dimensionality of superposed features in the Toy Models of Superposition sense.

rows.subject: TopK SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured per-concept sparsity on heterogeneous synthetic clusters.
rows.measure: Average number of active latents per data point, by concept
rows.value: Same level of sparsity per concept for all concepts
rows.note: The fixed sparsity does not adapt to the different intrinsic dimensions.
rows.check: Relink from V6 to V5. The cluster dimensions (6–126) are designed into synthetic data, so the row cannot bear on whether a model's features are 1-D. It measures whether the SAE adapts to concept geometry, and TopK shows no per-concept adaptation.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V5 from this measure alone. TopK uses the same sparsity for all concepts; reconstruction failure depends on K relative to concept dimension, as separately measured in R8.

rows.subject: TopK SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured normalized reconstruction error on heterogeneous synthetic clusters.

rows.note: The text gives the d = 6 example and says the same pattern holds for the other dimensions.
rows.check: Relink from V6 to V5. This is TopK reconstruction failure on designed data, not a measurement of model features. Normalized MSE falls below 20% only when k exceeds the concept's dimension.

relationships.condition: ReLU, JumpReLU and TopK SAEs on concepts that violate their geometric assumptions (synthetic, PCFG Transformer, DINOv2)
relationships.reason: Each architecture misses or mixes concepts: ReLU/JumpReLU F1 ≤0.5 on the nonseparable concept (R2, R4); TopK fails on high-dimensional concepts (R5, R7, R8); latents co-occur across PoS and classes (R13, R14, R16, R18).
relationships.display_finding: ReLU and JumpReLU SAEs reached an F1 of at most 0.5 on the nonseparable concept, TopK failed on high-dimensional concepts, and latents co-occurred across parts of speech and classes.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: ReLU, JumpReLU and TopK SAEs on concepts that violate their geometric assumptions (synthetic, PCFG Transformer, DINOv2)
source_check.reason: The authors explicitly report failure to capture concepts and lack of concept specialization under mismatched assumptions. R2/R4 document nonseparable-concept failure; R8 documents TopK's dimension-dependent reconstruction failure; R16/R18 document cross-concept co-occurrence. R5 concerns separability, not high-dimensional concepts.

relationships.condition: SAE whose architecture matches concept geometry (SpaDE), or linearly separable concepts for ReLU/JumpReLU
relationships.reason: Clean concept recovery occurs only when encoder assumptions fit the data: F1=1 for separable concepts (R1, R3) and for SpaDE (R6, R11, R12, R17). So recovered units depend on the architecture choice.
relationships.display_finding: Concept recovery reached F1 = 1 only for linearly separable concepts with ReLU/JumpReLU, or when the SpaDE architecture fit the geometry, so the recovered units depend on the architecture chosen.

relation.reason: The study directly evaluates concept recovery and architectural failure modes using synthetic ground truth, PCFG-model activations and DINOv2 activations.

tranche.reason: Theoretical receptive-field analysis and recovery experiments show that SAE architectures can miss or mix concepts when their geometric assumptions fail, directly qualifying V5.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased; SpaDE also imposes geometric assumptions and is not claimed universally optimal. PCFG baselines use best-of-sweep selection, with top-20 in Figure 7 versus top-10 in Appendix C.3; dictionary stability, canonicality and feature irreducibility are untested.

reader_labels.condition: Synthetic separability, heterogeneous-cluster, formal-language, and vision experiments
reader_labels.reason: The reported recovery varies with SAE architecture: some architectures miss or mix concepts that another SAE recovers, which challenges the idea that SAE features are universally complete or canonical (R2, R4-R8, R12-R14, R16-R18).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Heterogeneous synthetic clusters and formal-language model activations
reader_labels.reason: Concepts are reported to have different intrinsic dimensions, including clusters designed with dimensions 6, 14, 30, 62, and 126, and parts of speech with differing effective dimensions (R7-R11, R15).
